name: Ordinary activities and extraordinary items
definition: Ordinary activities are activities undertaken as part of the enterprise's business and related activities incidental to or arising from them. Extraordinary items are income or expenses arising from events or transactions clearly distinct from those ordinary activities and therefore not expected to recur frequently or regularly. Net profit or loss for the period comprises profit or loss from ordinary activities and extraordinary items, each disclosed on the face of the statement of profit and loss.
why_it_exists: The split tells a reader which part of the result is repeatable. Because the test is relative to the business each enterprise ordinarily carries on, the same event can be extraordinary for one enterprise and ordinary for another — so the classification cannot be read off the event type alone.
inputs: the nature of the event or transaction
the business ordinarily carried on by this enterprise
the amount of the income or expense
outputs: classification as profit or loss from ordinary activities, or as an extraordinary item
separate disclosure of the nature and amount of each extraordinary item
preconditions: an item of income or expense has been recognised in the period
exceptions: an item within ordinary activities that is of such size, nature or incidence that its disclosure is relevant to explain the performance of the enterprise is disclosed separately, without becoming an extraordinary item
common_mistakes: classifying by event type instead of by the enterprise's own ordinary activities — AS 5 paragraph 10 makes the test relative to the business ordinarily carried on
using frequency of occurrence as the test, when AS 5 paragraph 10 states the test is the nature of the event in relation to the business, not the frequency
treating a large or unusual ordinary item as extraordinary, when AS 5 paragraph 12 provides separate disclosure within ordinary activities for exactly that case
legal_references: UNKNOWN — statutory backing not extracted; only ICAI AS-1 and AS-5 were read for this claim, so no statute is cited
icai_references: AS 5, paragraph 4, definitions of ordinary activities and extraordinary items
gst_references: NOT APPLICABLE — AS-1 and AS-5 govern financial-statement policy and period attribution; GST is a separate determination and must not be conflated with it
evidence_required: a description of the event or transaction sufficient to judge its nature
a description of the business the enterprise ordinarily carries on
confidence_factors: weak when the enterprise's ordinary activities are not known, because the test is relative to them and cannot be applied without them
AS 5 states extraordinary items arise only on rare occasions, so a classification producing them routinely is itself a signal of error
AS 5 gives no threshold for the 'size, nature or incidence' that triggers separate disclosure under paragraph 12
validation_checks: the classification was decided by the nature of the event in relation to this enterprise's business, not by how often such events occur
each extraordinary item's nature and amount is separately disclosed in the statement of profit and loss
both components — profit or loss from ordinary activities, and extraordinary items — are disclosed on the face of the statement
examples: AS 5 paragraph 11 names attachment of property of the enterprise, and an earthquake, as events generally giving rise to extraordinary items for most enterprises
counterexamples: claims from policyholders arising from an earthquake are NOT extraordinary for an insurance enterprise that insures against such risks — the same event, the opposite classification, because the ordinary activities differ
